'''''Ulva clathrata''''' is a species of [[seaweed]] in the family [[Ulvaceae]] that can be found in such [[Europe]]an countries as [[Azores]], [[Belgium]], [[Ireland]], [[Netherlands]], and the [[United Kingdom]]. It is also common in [[Asia]]n and [[Africa]]n countries such as [[Israel]], [[Kenya]], [[Mauritius]], [[South Africa]], [[Tanzania]],<ref name=worms/> [[Japan]], [[Portugal]] and [[Tunisia]]. It has distribution in the [[Americas]] as well including [[Alaska]], [[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], [[Cuba]], [[Grenada]], [[Hispaniola]], and [[Venezuela]].<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.algaebase.org/search/species/detail/?species_id=48814|title=''Ulva clathrata'' (Roth) C.Agardh|publisher=[[AlgaeBase]]|accessdate=March 24, 2013}}</ref> Besides various countries it can be found in certain gulfs, oceans and seas such as the [[Gulf of Maine]] and [[Gulf of Mexico]], [[Indian Ocean]] and European waters (including [[Mediterranean Sea]]).<ref name=worms/>

==Description==
The plant is light green in colour and is {{convert|20|-|80|mm}} in height. The thin cylindrical threads are {{convert|1|-|3|mm}} in width.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/efsa/algae_revealed/pdf/Enteromorpha_clathrata.pdf|title=Enteromorpha (Ulva) clathrata (Roth) Greville|accessdate=March 24, 2013}}</ref>

==Uses==
It is used in [[biochemistry]], since it has 20-26% content of [[protein]], 32-36% of which are crude proteins. The plant also contains [[glucose]] (10–16%), [[rhamnose]] (36–40%), [[uronic acid]]s (27–29%), and [[xylose]] (10–13%).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Alberto Peña-Rodrígueza|author2=Thomas P. Mawhinneyb |author3=Denis Ricque-Mariea |author4=L. Elizabeth Cruz-Suárez  |title=Chemical composition of cultivated seaweed Ulva clathrata (Roth) C. Agardh|location=Mexico |doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2011.04.104 |pmid=30634256|volume=129 |issue=2|journal=Food Chemistry |pages=491–498|year=2011|url=http://eprints.uanl.mx/11137/1/BetoChemical--s2.0-S0308814611006704-main.pdf }}</ref>
